<explanation>
Below is a step-by-step explanation of how to create a detailed system design diagram for Periphery—a Swift tool to identify unused code in projects. The focus is on capturing each major component and their relationships as reflected in both the file tree and README, so that the diagram communicates the complete internal architecture and external integrations.

1. Identify the Major Components:
   • Frontend & CLI: Represented by the Sources/Frontend directory. This is where the command‐line interface (including main.swift and various command handlers like ScanCommand, VersionCommand, etc.) initializes the tool, parses user inputs (or “guided setup”), and dispatches further processing.
   • Project Drivers: Shown in Sources/ProjectDrivers. These are responsible for interfacing with different build systems and projects (Bazel, SPM, Xcode) and setting up the environment to generate the index store.
   • Indexer: Under Sources/Indexer. This module collects source files, reads the index store, and builds an initial analysis pipeline with components like SourceFileCollector, JobPool, and specific indexers (e.g. SwiftIndexer, XibIndexer). This is the foundation for extracting declaration information.
   • Source Graph & Graph Mutators: Represented by Sources/SourceGraph and its subdirectories (Elements, Mutators). Here the tool transforms index store data and parsed source files into an in-memory graph. Additional mutators refine this graph (e.g., marking entry points, identifying unused declarations) by applying specific rules.
   • Syntax Analysis: Contained in Sources/SyntaxAnalysis. It dives deeper into source files (through visitors such as DeclarationSyntaxVisitor) to directly parse code segments for additional context (e.g. unused function parameters or protocol analysis).
   • PeripheryKit & Output Formatting: Shown in Sources/PeripheryKit, this module handles the formatting (CodeClimate, JSON, Xcode formats, etc.) for output and reporting unused code findings.
   • Xcode and Logger Support: Additional modules, such as Sources/XcodeSupport, augment integration with Xcode (and help in project setup via Xcode project schemes), while Sources/Logger manages logging and debugging output.
   • Build/Configuration Components: Configuration files (e.g., swiftlint.yml, .bazelrc, .dockerignore, and MODULE.bazel) and automation tasks under .mise/ and bazel/ further round out the automation, CI integrations, and build system adaptations.

2. Map the Relationships and Data Flow:
   • Command Flow: The diagram should show an arrow starting from the “CLI (Sources/Frontend)” component that sends configuration and commands to “Project Drivers.” The “Project Drivers” interface with external build systems (Bazel, SPM, Xcode) and pass the location of the generated index store.
   • Indexing & Graph Formation: From the build system preparation, control flows to the “Indexer” which collects data and passes it to the “Source Graph” builder. Here, “Syntax Analysis” components may be shown as a supporting element that refines the raw data.
   • Graph Mutation & Analysis: Within the “Source Graph” module, a sub-process labeled “Graph Mutators” (from Sources/SourceGraph/Mutators) adjusts the graph to mark entry points, prune unused declarations, and enforce rules (e.g. handling protocols, unused imports, redundant public declarations).
   • Output Generation: The refined graph information is then handed off to “PeripheryKit/Results” for formatting the output. An arrow from “PeripheryKit” then shows the result being relayed back to the “CLI” for display or optionally integrated with CI tools.
   • Logging & Diagnostics: Connect “Logger” to every major module (Frontend, Indexer, etc.) to indicate that logging is consistently used across execution.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Separation of Concerns: Clearly separate the CLI command parsing (Frontend), build system interfacing (Project Drivers), and core analysis (Indexer, Source Graph, Syntax Analysis). Each module has its defined responsibilities.
   • Layered Architecture: Visualize this as layers—from external interface (CLI and Configuration) to data collection (Indexer and Project Drivers), then to processing (Source Graph & Mutators), and finally to output (PeripheryKit/Results & Logger).
   • Integration Points: Note that integration with various build systems (Bazel, Xcode, SPM) is a key design element hence include “Bazel rules” and integration configuration in the diagram.
   • Extensibility: Indicate that modules such as the Graph Mutators and Output Formatters are plug-in points for extending functionality (for example, adding support for additional formatting or analysis features).

4. Include Relevant Technologies & Frameworks:
   • Swift Language is the primary technology.
   • Bazel, Xcode, and SPM are the build systems.
   • Configuration files (.bazelrc, .dockerignore, swiftlint.yml, etc.) are used to manage coding style, continuous integration, and build automation.

5. Guidelines for Drawing the Diagram:
   • Use distinct shapes or colors to distinguish between:
     – Frontend/CLI components (e.g., rectangles with a specific color).
     – Processing Components (Indexer, Source Graph & Mutators) can be drawn with another shape or hue.
     – Configuration/Integration components (Project Drivers, XcodeSupport, Bazel) can have their own notation.
   • Label each node clearly with the module or component name (e.g., “Sources/Frontend – CLI,” “Sources/Indexer – Indexer Module”).
   • Draw directional arrows to indicate the data flow:
     – From command input → build system interfacing → index collection → graph building/mutation → output formatting.
   • Annotate where important processes occur (for example, “Graph Mutators: Removing unused declarations” or “Syntax Analysis: Parsing for unused function parameters”).
   • Optionally add layers or swimlanes to group components by responsibility (for instance, “User Interaction”, “Data Collection”, “Core Analysis”, “Result Generation”).

6. Special Tailoring to This Project:
   • Since Periphery is a static analysis tool for Swift, your diagram should emphasize the flow from build-time indexing to in-memory graph analysis.
   • Highlight how external build systems feed the index store, and how the tool then internally transforms that store into a structured graph which is traversed for results.
   • Ensure that aspects of Xcode Integration (as detailed in the README) are denoted, perhaps as a side-process that describes how the tool can be integrated into Xcode build phases.

By following these steps and including clear labels, directional arrows showing dependency and data flow, distinct colors/shapes for different module types, and annotations on design patterns, the resulting system design diagram will be comprehensive and tailored specifically to the Periphery project’s architecture.
</explanation>
